PHYSICAL SCIENCE AND MATHEMATICAL CLUES IN THE MANIFESTO

After receiving the Unabomber's Manifesto, should the FBI have paid
special attention to suspects with training in the physical sciences,
engineering or mathematics?  

Consider paragraph 99 in the "SOME PRINCIPLES OF HISTORY" section of the
Manifesto.

99. Think of history as being the sum of two components: an erratic
   component that consists of unpredictable events that follow no
   discernible pattern, and a regular component that consists of
   long-term historical trends. Here we are concerned with the long-term
   trends.

This idea of a signal with a noise component superimposed on it comes
straight from the physical and engineering sciences.  The idea is also
found in electronics and would be somewhat familiar to students of social
sciences and the soft sciences, at least to the extent they were
concerned with performing measurements of quantities that varied over
time.  

By choosing this idea to help explain his theory of history, the
Unabomber points out his own familiarity with at least one of these
areas.  The next two paragraphs are also very revealing:

100. FIRST PRINCIPLE. If a SMALL change is made that affects a
   long-term historical trend, then the effect of that change will almost
   always be transitory - the trend will soon revert to its original
   state. (Example: A reform movement designed to clean up political
                                . . . .
   widespread social changes; a SMALL change in the society won't be
   enough.) If a small change in a long-term historical trend appears to
   be permanent, it is only because the change acts in the direction in
   which the trend is already moving, so that the trend is not altered
   but only pushed a step ahead.
  
101. The first principle is almost a tautology. If a trend were not
   stable with respect to small changes, it would wander at random rather
   than following a definite direction; in other words it would not be a
   long-term trend at all.

"Stability" is once again a concept occurring frequently in engineering
and the physical sciences but also in other areas including electronics. 
However, the idea of stability with respect to small changes from
equilibrium is not as common in areas outside engineering and the
physical sciences.  Yet this idea appears twice in the Unabomber's
discussion, first implicitly in "the trend will soon revert to its
original state" and later explicitly in "stable with respect to small
changes."


UNABOMBER'S MODEL OF HISTORICAL TRENDS

Let's try to flesh-out the analogy the Unabomber appears to be trying to
make.  Imagine one of those children's playground slides in the form of
the lower, semi-circular half of a large plastic tube.   If one were to
place a baseball in the slide near the top and release it, the ball would
follow a path down the center line of the slide.  That path would be the
long term trend the Unabomber is talking about.  

If one introduced a small change by lightly tapping the ball towards the
side as it was rolling down, the ball would be depart from the center
temporarily but eventually move back toward the center line of the slide
(and probably oscillate back and forth across the center line).  In
effect, the path the ball takes is stable with respect to the small
changes we make by tapping it lightly.

This is not the only way one can think about historical trends and it is
probably not a viewpoint many historians would accept.  Consider an
alternative analogy.

Imagine you are standing at the top of a rocky gully and you toss a
baseball down the gully.  Every time the ball strikes a rock on the way
down it will bounce off in a seemingly random direction.  If you make a
small change in the velocity of the ball as you toss it or while it is on
the way down, it will strike the next rock at a different spot and bounce
off in a very different direction than it would have without the small
change.  Subsequent bounces will likely be from an entirely different
series of rocks and the path will be quite different as a result of the
small change we made in the ball's velocity.

In the gully example, we don't have any sort of equilibrium path as we
had with the children's slide example but we can still make some
predictions about the behaviour of the ball based on the nature of the
gully and the forces acting on the ball.  For example, the ball will go
down the gully rather than up and the path tend to be somewhere near the
center of the gully in most cases.   

Historians (I suspect) would prefer the second analogy which permits
small changes to occasionally have significant effects.  After all, if
Adolf Hitler had been run over by a bus in 1920, would history really
have been the same?  The Unabomber's choice of the equilibrium type model
suggests he is not a historian but instead has as a technical or hard
science type background. 

PHRASES USED IN DESCRIPTION

The words and phrases the Unabomber used are also consistent with a
technical or hard sciences background: "sum of two components,"  "no
discernable pattern," "revert to its original state," and "stable with
respect to small changes."  

What's more, the Unabomber uses this technical jargon in appropriate
places and an apparently correct manner.  If the Unabomber was merely
cribbing technical phrases with which he wasn't familiar, we would expect
a few mistakes. 

The one phrase that doesn't quite fit with a technical or hard sciences
background is "The first principle is almost a tautology."  Although
"tautology" is occasionally used in theoretical areas of the physical
sciences it is much more common in mathematics and philosophical logic. 

Of course, we wouldn't be able to rule out the possibility that the
Unabomber had simply looked up the fancy word "tautology" in his
dictionary and included it in the Manifesto just to "show off" to his
audience.  


CONCLUSIONS

In paragraphs 99 - 101 of the Manifesto, the Unabomber clearly
demonstrates he is very familiar with ideas found primarily in the
physical sciences and in engineering and hence is likely to have had
training in one of these areas.  I wonder if the FBI's post-Manifesto
profile reflected this.
